queue.title: Spec loop R3 -- re-derive again, independently
queue.detail: DONE, iteration 6, and it did not come back empty either -- three rounds, three rounds that changed the proposal. THE FINDING: R1 and R2 both concluded that the third instance of F310 (DirectoryPicker inside ProjectManagerModal) was repaired by task 1.1 without an edit, because the picker already calls preventDefault() at :57-62. It cannot be. That handler is a React onKeyDown bound to the picker's root div (:85-91, tabIndex=-1) and nothing in the file ever focuses that root; opening the browser leaves focus on the Browse... button, a SIBLING of the picker (ProjectManagerModal.tsx:153 vs :157-166), so React never dispatches through the picker's subtree, preventDefault() never runs, and 1.1's defaultPrevented condition is false. The modal closes and takes the browser with it -- same visible cost as F310, different mechanism, which is why two rounds reading for outcome agreed on the wrong one. The change's own D3 had already argued exactly this in the opposite direction ('focus is frequently not inside the panel at all'). Written up as design.md D9: arbitration by defaultPrevented presumes the nested owner HOLDS THE KEYBOARD, and the precondition differs by mechanism -- Radix binds document/capture and is focus-independent, while a React onKeyDown only fires for a target inside its own subtree. Consequence for the other instance: the reason input's handler works only because task 4.1 focuses it, so the F310 half DEPENDS ON the F309 half -- now task 2.1a, because an implementer landing 1.1 and 2.1 alone would watch leg C3 still fail with no reason to suspect the focus work. Fix chosen over narrowing the scenario: 2.2 focuses the picker root on open (it already carries role=dialog and tabIndex=-1), 2.2a returns focus to the trigger on close so the repair does not import F307's shape, and 2.2b plus a D8 carve-out stop it being read as the general F307 fix. SECOND FINDING: the delta scenario 'Typing an answer does not operate the menu' had NO task producing its evidence in any round, and its second clause ('no part of the surface becomes unresponsive to the pointer') is FALSE of the correctly fixed product -- TaskDetailDrawer renders a fixed inset-0 scrim at :195-209 that deliberately makes the board unresponsive and that its own click-outside listener depends on. Narrowed to 'does not stop answering the pointer BECAUSE A MENU RE-OPENED over it', and given evidence by a new task 7.8 (the rowmenu harness's PROBE already reads both facts); 7.8a records that leg P5 is NOT that evidence, because it focuses the trigger by hand and passes before and after. ALSO: 7.4 rewritten to name the focus state it must drive FROM -- without clicking inside the browser first, since a leg that clicks a breadcrumb would pass against an unfixed picker; 7.4a added as the mutation-check for the task two rounds denied was needed; 7.4b drives 2.2a. ALSO (b): six existing hub-interaction-feedback requirements, not five, all read as bodies -- R2's 'all about appearance' verdict survives and neither ADDED requirement collides, but 'Keyboard focus is visible' is a shipped requirement that 4.1's swap from autoFocus to a programmatic .focus() is one implementation away from breaching, so 4.1a guards it and 7.6 drives it. openspec validate --strict passes; openspec list reads 0/40 tasks, up from 32.

The trap R2 found is worth generalising, and D-5 should describe its shape: a proposal can be right about the code and still write a DELTA THAT CLAIMS MORE THAN THE CHANGE DELIVERS. The over-claim rides in on a scenario's WHEN clause rather than on any statement about the code, so a round that only re-checks source citations cannot see it. The test that catches it is: name the task that produces this scenario's evidence, then ask whether it can.

R3 (iteration 6) generalised the trap R2 found, and D-5 should state the general form once: a proposal can be right about the code and still write a delta that CLAIMS MORE THAN THE CHANGE DELIVERS (R2's finding, and R3's DirectoryPicker finding) or that a SHIPPED BEHAVIOUR CONTRADICTS (R3's scrim finding). Neither rides in on a statement about the code, so a round that only re-checks source citations cannot see either. The test that catches both: name the task that produces this scenario's evidence and ask whether it CAN -- then, if the answer is yes, ask what already-shipped behaviour would make the scenario false.

A round that re-reads what the previous round already re-read is the low-yield round.
